id: My Daughter at the Gymnastics Party

prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

When I sat for a moment in the bleachers of the lower-school gym to watch, one by one, the girls of my daughter’s kindergarten climb the fat rope hung over the Styrofoam pit, I remembered my sweet exasperated mother and those shifting faces of injury that followed me like an odor to ball games and practices, playgrounds of monkey bars and trampolines, those wilted children sprouting daily in that garden of trauma behind her eyes. Then Rachel’s turn, the smallest child in class, and up she went, legs twined on the rope, ponytail swinging, fifteen, twenty, twenty-five feet, the pink tendrils of her leotard climbing without effort until she’d cleared the lower rafters. She looked down, then up, hanging in that balance of pride and fear, then glancing toward the bleachers to see if I watched, let go her left hand, unworried by that boy with the waffled skull, stiff and turning blue under the belly of a horse, or the Christmas Eve skater on Cagle’s Lake, her face a black plum against the bottom of the ice.

outputs.L2:
Perched briefly on the gym bleachers of the elementary school, I watched the kindergarten girls take turns scaling the thick rope suspended above the foam landing pit, and found myself thinking of my mother—kind yet endlessly frustrated—and how visions of injured children trailed her constantly, like a persistent scent, wherever we went: to games, to practices, to playgrounds full of jungle gyms and trampolines. Behind her eyes lived a private garden where damaged children bloomed fresh each day.

Then it was Rachel's turn. Being the tiniest one in her class, she wrapped her legs around the rope and began ascending anyway, her ponytail bouncing as she rose—fifteen feet, then twenty, then twenty-five—the pink fabric of her leotard drifting upward with apparent ease until she'd passed beneath the lower ceiling beams. She glanced downward, then up again, suspended somewhere between confidence and terror, before checking the bleachers to confirm I was watching. Then she released her left hand, indifferent to the memory of that boy with the dented skull who'd gone rigid and blue beneath a horse's stomach, or the girl who'd skated on Cagle's Lake that Christmas Eve, her face like a dark bruised fruit pressed against the underside of the ice.
outputs.L3:
# The Weight We Carry

I remember my mother's face at every ball game, every practice, every trip to the playground—that particular tightness around her eyes, the way her hands would find each other and clasp, knuckles whitening, as she watched us run and jump and climb with the reckless abandon only children possess. She never said much. She didn't have to. Her worry lived in the set of her shoulders, in how she'd lean forward on the bleachers as if proximity alone might catch a falling child, might somehow soften whatever catastrophe her mind had already conjured. I used to think she was simply overprotective, a woman who saw danger in monkey bars and shadows in swimming pools. Now I understand she was carrying something heavier than caution—she was carrying the accumulated weight of every terrible thing she'd ever heard happen to a child, waiting, always waiting, for the world to prove her right.

Today, I sit in bleachers of my own, watching my daughter Rachel—barely five, the smallest child in her kindergarten class—approach a thick rope suspended from the gymnasium ceiling. The gym teacher has arranged this exercise as something joyful, a test of strength and determination, but I feel my mother's old anxiety stirring in my own chest, an inheritance I never asked for but recognize instantly, like a family heirloom passed down through blood rather than choice.

Rachel wraps her small hands around the rope and begins to climb.

She moves with a confidence that startles me—an ease that seems impossible given her size, given how her feet barely reach past her classmates' shoulders when she stands in line. Hand over hand, knees gripping, she ascends steadily, gracefully, as though gravity has granted her some special exemption. The other children below seem to shrink as she climbs higher, and I find myself holding my breath, watching this fragment of myself suspended between floor and ceiling, between safety and something else entirely.

Near the top, she pauses. I can see it even from here—the moment where pride and fear collide in her small body, where the thrill of having climbed so high meets the sudden awareness of how far down the ground has become. She hangs there, suspended in that particular equilibrium children discover before they learn to name it, and then she turns her head, searching the bleachers, searching for me.

I lift my hand. I don't know if she can see me, whether the distance and the gymnasium lights obscure her view, but I keep my hand raised anyway, because I understand instinctively what she needs in this moment—not rescue, not intervention, just witness. Just the knowledge that someone is watching, that someone will remember this small triumph.

She lets go with one hand.

It's a simple gesture, really—shifting her weight, testing her balance, showing herself and perhaps showing me that she trusts her own grip, her own strength. But watching her do it, I feel my mother's old fear rising in me like floodwater, and beneath it, unbidden, come the memories I've spent years trying not to excavate: the boy from my elementary school who drowned during a birthday party while adults grilled hamburgers twenty feet away; the girl who fell from monkey bars and never quite walked the same way again; the countless smaller tragedies that never made the news but lived instead in whispered conversations between mothers, cautionary tales meant to justify the tightness in their shoulders, the way they never looked away.

I think of my mother now, and I understand her differently than I ever did as a child. She wasn't simply anxious—she was translating love into vigilance, transforming her fear into a kind of protective magic, as if watching closely enough might ward off disaster through sheer force of attention. I used to resent that watchfulness, that constant hovering presence at the edges of my childhood. Now, watching Rachel balance one-handed at the top of a rope, thirty feet above a gymnasium floor, I feel that same magical thinking overtake me: if I watch closely enough, if I never look away, she will be safe. She has to be safe.

Rachel finds my face in the bleachers, and something in her expression shifts—the fear recedes slightly, replaced by pure, uncomplicated joy. She grins, this small triumphant creature dangling above the world, entirely unaware of the darkness I carry, the catalog of tragedies I've involuntarily compiled over decades of being someone's child and now someone's parent. She doesn't know about drowned boys or broken bones or all the ways childhood can turn suddenly, irrevocably wrong. She only knows that she climbed higher than she thought possible, that her mother is watching, that for this moment, she is invincible.

I smile back at her, burying my fear beneath something that must look, from this distance, like simple pride. Because that's the inheritance I want to give her—not my mother's constant vigil, not the weight of every tragedy I've ever imagined, but this: the belief that she can climb as high as she wants, that letting go with one hand is not reckless but brave, that the world, despite everything, might still be safe enough to explore.

She begins her descent, confident and unafraid, and I finally release the breath I didn't know I'd been holding, understanding now what my mother must have understood all those years ago: that watching your child navigate the world's dangers requires a peculiar kind of faith, one that exists precisely because certainty is impossible, one that chooses hope not because fear has been conquered, but despite the fact that it never quite goes away.
outputs.L4:
# The Rope

My mother used to say that having children meant carrying a permanent bruise on your heart—one that never quite healed, just shifted location depending on which child was doing what dangerous thing at any given moment. She'd catalogued decades of small catastrophes: my brother's collarbone snapping like a green twig off the Hendersons' fence, the Delacroix girl who nearly drowned in four feet of water because no one was watching for the ninety seconds it takes for a child to slip beneath the surface, the boy two streets over who lost partial vision in one eye from a poorly aimed dart. She kept these stories the way other people keep photographs, pulling them out at odd moments—watching me climb a ladder to clean gutters, watching my own children run across a parking lot—as if reciting them might ward off their repetition.

I didn't understand this vigilance until I had Rachel, and even then, understanding came slowly, in pieces, the way most real knowledge does.

Today I am standing in the gymnasium of her kindergarten, arms crossed against the particular chill of institutional buildings, watching my daughter approach a thick knotted rope that hangs from the ceiling like some challenge from an older, harder world. She is easily the smallest child in her class—a fact the pediatrician mentions at every visit with the practiced neutrality of someone delivering information that is not quite bad news but requires acknowledgment nonetheless. She comes up to the shoulders of most of her classmates. Her hands, when she reaches for the rope, seem impossibly small against its thick braided width.

But she doesn't hesitate. This is the thing I notice first, before the fear arrives: she doesn't pause the way I might expect a small child to pause before an obstacle clearly designed with larger bodies in mind. She simply reaches up, grips the rope with both hands, and begins to climb, her sneakers finding purchase against the knots with a confidence that seems to belong to someone else entirely—some braver, larger version of my daughter that exists only in these moments of physical daring.

She climbs three feet, then five, her small frame swinging slightly with each pull upward. I feel my mother's old vigilance rising in me like floodwater, some ancient parental sonar pinging out warnings: *too high, too small, what if her grip slips, what if she falls, what if—*

And there it is. The catalogue opens itself in my mind unbidden, the way it always does: a college roommate who fell from a similar rope during a gym class decades ago, shattering his wrist in a way that required three surgeries and left him unable to fully straighten his arm for the rest of his life. A news story from years back about a playground accident, the kind of story you read once and then carry forever, filed away in that part of the brain reserved for things that could happen to your own children. My mother's voice, imagined now, saying *be careful, be careful*, the words worn smooth from years of repetition until they'd become less warning than prayer.

This is what nobody tells you about parenthood: that it recalibrates your relationship to gravity itself, to every hard surface and sharp edge, to the fundamental instability of a world that seemed, before children, merely neutral, and now seems actively conspiring toward harm. You start to see the specific danger in playground equipment, in swimming pools, in kitchen knives left carelessly on countertops, in the particular slope of a staircase. The world doesn't change, but your eyes do—they become permanently tuned to threat, to the thousand small ways a small body might be broken.

Rachel climbs another foot, her face set in an expression of fierce concentration that I recognize from other contexts—her tackling a jigsaw puzzle, or trying to tie her shoes for the first time. This is her serious face, the one that means she has decided something is important and worth the effort of full attention.

Then, six feet up, she turns her head and finds me in the small crowd of parents gathered at the gymnasium's edge.

She grins.

It's not a look of triumph, exactly, or even excitement—it's simpler than that, more essential. It's the look of a child who wants her father to witness this moment of small conquest, who needs the accomplishment reflected back through someone else's eyes to make it fully real. *Look at me,* the grin says. *Look what I'm doing.* There is no fear in her face at all, none of the vertigo I feel watching her from below, no awareness of how far six feet might seem to a body that stands barely three feet tall when planted on solid ground.

This is the strange gift of childhood, I think—this capacity to attempt dangerous, difficult things without the full weight of consequence pressing down on the decision. Rachel doesn't know yet what it means to break a bone, hasn't experienced the specific vulnerability of a body that can be damaged in ways both temporary and permanent. She has fallen before, of course—the ordinary scrapes and bruises of childhood, the skinned knee from a bicycle mishap, the bumped head from an ill-timed game of tag—but nothing that has taught her caution as a fundamental orientation toward the world. She still believes, in the unconscious way of small children, that she is essentially indestructible, that ropes and heights and physical daring exist primarily as opportunities rather than threats.

I smile back at her, giving her the affirmation she's seeking, even as some other part of me continues its silent calculation of angles and distances, of what exactly would happen if her grip failed at this particular height. This is the strange doubling of parenthood: to smile encouragement while internally rehearsing catastrophe, to celebrate courage while cataloguing every way that courage might lead to harm.

She climbs another two feet—reaching now what I estimate to be eight feet off the ground, though estimation is difficult from this angle—before the gym teacher calls out that it's time to come down, that she's done wonderfully, that it's someone else's turn. Rachel begins her descent with the same fearless confidence she showed climbing up, though descending is, in my experience, always the more treacherous direction—the moment when fatigue meets gravity, when the adrenaline of ascent gives way to the harder physics of controlled falling.

She reaches the ground safely. Of course she does. This is what I have to remind myself: that most climbs end without incident, that most children navigate these small dangers successfully, that my mother's catalogue of accidents represents the statistical exception rather than the rule, however vivid those exceptions remain in memory.

Rachel runs toward me across the gymnasium floor, her face lit with the particular joy of a child who has done something hard and done it well. "Did you see me, Daddy? Did you see how high I went?"

"I saw," I tell her, crouching down to her level, feeling the specific ache of love that comes with watching your child succeed at something slightly frightening. "You were so brave."

She beams at this, brave being a word she's recently learned to value, something she heard in a book or a movie and has been trying on for size ever since, testing whether it fits.

Standing back up, I watch her run off to rejoin her classmates, this small fierce person who carries none of the accumulated weight of accident and injury that lives in my own mind, none of my mother's careful catalogue of childhood catastrophe. She simply climbed a rope today, growing an inch taller in confidence, learning something about her own capability that she'll carry forward into other small daring acts.

I think again of my mother's old phrase—the permanent bruise on the heart—and understand now that this is not quite right, or not complete. It is not only fear that parents carry forward through their children's lives, watching each small danger with held breath. It is also this: the privilege of witnessing courage in its purest form, uncomplicated by consequence, undiminished by the knowledge of what might go wrong. Rachel's fearlessness on that rope was not naivety exactly, though it contained elements of not-yet-knowing. It was something closer to grace—the capacity to attempt difficult things simply because they present themselves as worth attempting, without the paralytic weight of imagined catastrophe.

I carry my mother's catalogue of accidents, yes, will likely carry it for the rest of my life, adding new entries as I witness new dangers navigate by my own children. But I am learning also to carry this other thing: the specific wonder of watching a child climb toward something difficult, glancing back to make sure someone she loves is watching, unburdened by fear in a way I can barely remember being myself.

Vulnerability and courage, then, not as opposites but as necessary companions—the same small body capable of both extraordinary daring and profound fragility, sometimes within the same six seconds of climbing a rope in a school gymnasium on an otherwise unremarkable Tuesday morning. This is what I witnessed today, watching my daughter climb toward the ceiling with her impossibly small hands: not just a child conquering a minor physical challenge, but something like a preview of every future moment when she will reach for something difficult, will risk falling in pursuit of some higher purchase, will look back to make sure someone who loves her is watching, ready to celebrate her bravery even while quietly, privately, hoping she doesn't fall.
outputs.L5:
# When Styrofoam, Then...

When Styrofoam first appeared on the market in the mid-20th century, it seemed like a miracle material. Lightweight, cheap to produce, and remarkably effective at insulation, it quickly found its way into countless products—from coffee cups to packaging materials to building insulation.

When Styrofoam is used for a coffee cup that holds your morning drink for perhaps twenty minutes, then that same cup will persist in the environment for centuries afterward. This stark imbalance between fleeting utility and enduring consequence lies at the heart of growing concerns about the material.

When Styrofoam breaks down, it doesn't decompose in any meaningful sense. Instead, it fragments into smaller and smaller pieces called microplastics, then these particles infiltrate soil, waterways, and eventually the food chain. Marine life often mistakes these fragments for food, then suffers the physical consequences of ingesting indigestible material.

When communities began recognizing these environmental costs, then many started taking action. Cities and countries around the world have implemented bans or restrictions on Styrofoam products, particularly single-use items like food containers and packaging peanuts. When such policies take effect, then businesses must adapt by seeking alternatives—compostable containers, paper-based packaging, or reusable systems.

When we consider the full lifecycle of Styrofoam, then the true cost becomes clear: a material designed for momentary convenience creates a legacy of pollution that far outlasts its usefulness. The challenge now lies in developing truly sustainable alternatives that can match Styrofoam's practical benefits without its devastating environmental footprint.

When innovation meets necessity, then perhaps we'll find solutions that serve both human needs and planetary health.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a literary short piece about watching my daughter climb a rope in gym class, weaving in memories of childhood injuries and fear passed down from my mother.
counterfactuals.output:
# Rope

The gymnasium smells like it always has—rubber and chalk and something underneath that might be fear, might be floor wax. I sit on the bottom bleacher with my knees pulled up, watching my daughter stand at the base of the climbing rope, her hands already reaching for it before the teacher finishes explaining the rules.

She is eight. Her hair is in the braid I did this morning, too tight, the way she likes it so it doesn't come loose. I remember braiding my own hair like that once, alone in the bathroom, because my mother's hands shook too much by then to do it for me.

The rope hangs from a beam thirty feet up, thick as a wrist, knotted every few feet like a spine. My daughter grips it low, wraps her legs around it the way she was taught, and looks back at me—just once—before she starts to climb.

I want to call out *be careful.* The words are already in my throat, worn smooth from use, my mother's words before they were mine. *Be careful* on the swing set. *Be careful* on the second stair, the one that creaked. *Be careful* climbing into the maple tree in the backyard, though I did it anyway, at nine, and fell twenty feet through branches that broke my fall and then my arm, a green branch snapping under me like a joint.

I remember the sound more than the pain. A wet crack, close to my ear, like biting into something that wasn't ready to be eaten. My mother's face when she came running—not concern first, but a kind of vindication, as if the break confirmed something she'd always known about the world. *I told you,* she said, in the emergency room, stroking my hair while the doctor set the bone. *I told you to be careful.*

She had her own rope, once. I only heard about it in pieces, the way you hear about a country before you're born there. A rope in a barn, a hayloft, a fall that broke something in her hip that never set right, that made her walk with a hitch for the rest of her life, that she blamed—not on the barn, not on the rope, not on the eleven-year-old girl she'd been—but on some careless quality in herself she was terrified she'd passed down. She saw it in me constantly. Every skinned knee was evidence. Every bruise, a prophecy fulfilling itself.

I did not want to inherit her fear the way I inherited her hands, her low voice, the way we both go quiet when we're hurting instead of loud. But fear moves through blood like anything else. It doesn't ask permission.

My daughter is six feet up now. Her arms shake slightly with the effort—I can see it from here, that fine tremor of muscle not yet grown into itself—and my own chest tightens in sympathy, or memory, or both. I think of the branch. I think of my mother's hip, the way she'd wince getting out of the car for thirty years afterward, a full and physical wince, and how I used to watch her face for it, waiting, as if her pain were weather I needed to track.

I do not call out *be careful.*

I say nothing at all, which costs me something I can't name.

My daughter climbs another few feet, her sneakers finding the knots by instinct now, not looking down, not looking at me. The gym teacher stands below with his arms crossed, unworried, the way you're unworried about things that are not your own children. I envy him that unworry the way I've envied strangers on planes, sleeping through turbulence I white-knuckle through.

She reaches the top. She reaches up and slaps the beam, the way the other kids did before her, a small triumphant sound, skin on painted wood, and then she is grinning down at all of us, at me, and I realize I have been holding my breath since she left the ground.

She descends faster than she climbed, sliding the last few feet, landing with a small thud that makes my stomach drop even though I can see she is fine, she is laughing, she is already running to tell me *did you see, did you see,* and I say yes, yes I saw, and I mean to sound proud, and I think I do, mostly.

But some old fear in me is still climbing down slowly, still gripping the rope too tight, still hearing a branch that broke thirty years ago and a hip that never healed right and a voice saying *I told you* like it was armor instead of what it really was—a woman standing in the wreckage of her own careful life, trying to keep her daughter from falling anywhere at all.

I hug my daughter. Her heart is going fast under her shirt, from climbing, from joy, not from fear. Not yet. Not from me.

I will try to keep it that way as long as I can.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a lyrical, first-person paragraph that blends a present-tense scene of a kindergarten gymnastics class with intrusive memories of past accidents and death.
counterfactuals.output: The mats smell like rubber and spilled juice, and I count heads—one two three four five six seven, all present, all breathing—while Mrs. Okafor claps the beat for somersaults. I watch Lily's small feet leave the ground and something in my chest lurches sideways, back to another gymnasium, another fall that didn't end in giggles and chalk dust but in sirens and a stillness I still taste when I close my eyes. Roll, tuck, land—I say the words like a prayer, like if I repeat them enough they'll drown out the sound of a skull meeting concrete, a sound that lives in me now the way a splinter lives under skin, forgotten until pressed. The children shriek with delight over nothing, over everything, over the simple miracle of their bodies obeying gravity and then defying it, and I clap too, I clap so hard my palms sting, because clapping is easier than remembering the weight of a small body that never got up, never got its ribbon for participation, never got older. Seven heads. I count again. Marcus wobbles on the beam and my hand shoots out before I've even decided to move, muscle memory built from all the times I was too slow, too far, too late—and he steadies himself, laughing, unaware that I just relived a funeral in the space between his stumble and his balance. The tumbling mats are a soft blue, the color of the sky the day we buried someone too young, and I fold that thought away like laundry, like something to be dealt with later, because right now there's a circle to form, a song about a beanbag, small hands reaching for mine, and I have to be here, fully here, even as the past keeps tugging at my sleeve like a child who wants to show me one more thing.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a piece of creative nonfiction in dense, poetic prose about parental anxiety, using vivid, unsettling imagery of childhood injuries juxtaposed with a tender moment of watching a child succeed.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Weight of Small Bones

There is a catalog I keep, unwilling, in the soft tissue behind my sternum: the sound of skull meeting hardwood, that particular hollow knock like knuckles on a door no one wants answered. The way blood looks impossibly bright against a white bathroom tile, more red than red should be, a red that seems to announce itself, *look what I have done to your daughter's lip.* I have memorized the exact pitch of a child's scream when the scream means *real* and not *attention*, that register that bypasses the ears entirely and goes straight for the gut, straight for the place where you keep your own animal terror.

I think of femurs. I think of the word *greenstick*, how doctors say it so gently, as if the fracture itself were something tender, something growing. I think of the soft spot on an infant's head, that impossible negotiation between protection and vulnerability, bone that hasn't yet decided to be bone. I have held my son's head like an egg I was afraid to bruise, felt the pulse there, felt how thin the membrane is between *here* and *gone*, between *fine* and the great white nothing of an emergency room waiting area at 3 a.m., those chairs bolted to the floor as if grief might otherwise carry them away.

This is the tax we pay for loving something that runs before it looks, that climbs before it calculates, that trusts gravity like gravity has ever been anyone's friend.

But watch—

watch her now, seven years old, standing at the edge of the pool with her whole small body coiled like a question mark, and she is not thinking about her tibia, about the concrete lip six inches from where she'll enter the water, about all the ways a body can fail a body. She is thinking only: *now*. And she jumps—not falls, not stumbles, but *chooses*—and for one suspended second she is entirely airborne, entirely hers, no longer the sum of my fears but simply a girl becoming a cannonball, becoming a small localized explosion of joy, and the water opens for her like it has been waiting, like it recognizes her as someone who belongs to motion, to risk, to the profound arrogance of being young and unbroken.

She surfaces laughing. Chlorine-stung eyes, hair plastered like seaweed, and she is *shining*, she is incandescent with the fact of her own daring, and I am standing at the edge in my regular clothes with my heart doing something complicated and enormous, some geological shift between terror and grace, because this—*this*—is what all that vigilance was for. Not to keep her small and safe and stationary but to let her arrive, soaking and radiant, at this exact moment of unafraid.

I clap. I cannot help it. Some animal part of me, the same part that catalogs the sound of falling, now catalogs this instead: the particular music of her triumph, filed away next to all the other things I am helpless to protect and helpless not to love.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Draft a single long, flowing sentence-style narrative passage about a parent's complicated feelings—pride, fear, inherited worry—while watching their small child perform a physical feat at school.
counterfactuals.output: The morning she climbed to the top of the knotted rope in the gymnasium, hand over hand, sneakers scrabbling against the coarse fiber, her whole small body a fist of determination, I felt something in my chest fold and unfold at the same time, a pride so sharp it was nearly indistinguishable from fear, because there she was, seven years old and weightless with confidence, reaching for a rafter I had spent my whole childhood being warned away from by a mother who saw danger in every height, every edge, every game that asked a body to trust itself, and I had absorbed that warning so thoroughly that it had become a kind of inheritance, a worry passed hand to hand like the rope itself, so that even now, decades later, standing at the edge of the gym with the other parents clapping and calling out encouragement, I could feel my own mother's voice rising in my throat, telling me to tell her to come down, to be careful, to not trust her arms so completely to something that could let go, and yet I said nothing, because some other voice, newer and more fragile, was insisting that I let this be hers, this triumph, this single unguarded moment of a child believing her body was capable of anything, and so I watched her ring the little brass bell at the top with her open palm, watched her grin flash down at me like sunlight breaking water, and I clapped until my hands stung, swallowing the old fear whole, letting it sit heavy and familiar in my stomach beside the pride, because I understood, watching her descend now with the same fierce concentration, that I would carry both of these forever, the wanting to shield her from every fall and the wanting to watch her climb anyway, and that this contradiction was not a flaw in my love but the exact shape of it, worry and wonder knotted together like the rope she'd just conquered, impossible to separate, impossible to hand down any differently than it had been handed to me.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write in the style of literary fiction: a father recalls disturbing images of injured or dead children from his past while his daughter climbs a rope in gym class, ending on a moment of suspended tension.
counterfactuals.output:
The gymnasium smelled of rubber and pennies, that particular sweat-and-varnish smell that never changed no matter how many years passed since he'd last stood in one. Marcus sat on the bleacher's lowest rung, knees too high, hands folded like a man in church, and watched his daughter chalk her palms.

The rope hung from the rafters, thick as a wrist, swaying almost imperceptibly in the current from the ceiling fans. Sara stood beneath it in her gray gym shorts, nine years old and narrow as a reed, waiting for the whistle.

He thought of the boy in Kandahar. He hadn't meant to. It arrived the way these things always did, unbidden, sideways, a photograph developing in acid. The boy had been perhaps seven, lying in the rubble with one leg bent wrong beneath him, and Marcus had been twenty-four then, a medic, and he had knelt in the dust and understood immediately that there was nothing to be done. The boy's eyes had found his and held them with an expression Marcus had spent fifteen years trying not to name.

The whistle blew. Sara jumped, caught the rope in both hands, and began to climb.

He watched her feet find purchase, the rope wrapping once around her ankle in the technique they'd taught her, foot-lock and pull, foot-lock and pull. Her arms were thin. He remembered—he could not stop the remembering—the girl on the Interstate, the one in the median after the crash, no older than six, her shoe forty feet away in the grass as though she'd stepped clean out of it, and how the paramedics had moved with that particular unhurried speed people use when hurrying no longer matters.

Sara was three feet up now. Four. Her face was set in the concentration of a much older person, tongue between her teeth, and he made himself see only that: the tongue, the chalk dust rising off her palms in small clouds, the ordinary gymnasium light falling gray through the high windows.

He had held children who lived, too—that was the thing no one warned you about, that the living ones haunted differently than the dead, because you never knew what became of them, whether the trembling stopped, whether they slept through nights, whether some grown version of them sat now in some other gymnasium watching some other child climb toward the ceiling. He had held a boy's hand for eleven minutes once, waiting for transport, humming something tuneless, and the boy had lived, and Marcus had never learned his name, and this not-knowing had become its own kind of scar tissue, smooth and unremarkable until pressed.

Sara was seven feet up. Eight. The rope creaked against its bracket.

Around him other parents watched with the mild, forgettable attention of people who had never seen what rope could do, what falling could do, what an inch of difference in the angle of a small skull against pavement could do. They checked their phones. One woman laughed softly at something on her screen. Marcus's hands, still folded, had gone white at the knuckle.

Sara's coach called out, "Good, Sara, nice and easy," and the ordinariness of this—nice and easy, as though anything about ten feet of empty air below a child's dangling sneakers could be nice, could be easy—struck him with a force that closed his throat.

She was nine feet up now, ten, nearing the taped mark on the rope that meant she could stop, could ring the little bell bolted to the beam and begin her controlled descent. Her arms trembled faintly. He could see it from the bleachers, the small tremor of exertion, and some old and terrible part of his mind superimposed onto her trembling arms the memory of another child's hand, shaking uncontrollably in his own gloved grip in a triage tent that no longer existed in any world except the one he carried folded inside his ribs.

She reached the tape. Her fingers grazed the small brass bell.

And there, for one suspended second before the sound came—before the thin, bright note rang out across the gymnasium and released something in his chest he hadn't known was clenched—Marcus sat perfectly still, watching his daughter hang ten feet above a mat that suddenly seemed impossibly thin, the whole of his life balanced, as she was, in that instant between reaching and ringing, between held breath and release, unable yet to tell which way the moment would fall.
